## R, in one slide {.smaller .deepdive run="tools"}

::: {.skiplink}
[R tutorial, 9 slides – skip to Hands-on 2 →](#hands-on-2-meet-the-emails-draw-the-graph)
:::

```{.r code-line-numbers="|1|3|5|7"}
n_emails <- 1014                  # <- assigns. "n_emails gets 1014"

mean(c(1, 0, 1, 1))               # a function: name, then arguments in ()

audit$reply                       # $ picks one column out of a data frame

audit |> nrow()                   # |> the pipe: send the left into the right
```

::: {.small}
With four pieces of syntax you can read most R: **assign** with `<-`, **call** a function with `name(...)`, **reach into** an object with `$`, and **chain** with the pipe `|>`.
:::

::: notes
If you have never written a line of R, this slide is most of what you need to read the rest. Four things. First, the arrow assigns: n emails gets one thousand and fourteen. You will see the equals sign used the same way and both work, but the arrow is the convention. Second, a function is a name followed by round brackets holding its arguments: the mean of one, nought, one and one, which is three quarters, and which is also how you get a share out of a column of zeros and ones. Third, the dollar sign reaches inside a data frame to pull out one column. And fourth, the pipe takes whatever is on its left and feeds it in as the first argument of whatever is on its right. Read it as the word "then", and long chains become sentences.
:::

## Getting data in {.smaller .deepdive run="tools"}

```{.r code-line-numbers="|1|3"}
audit <- readr::read_csv("data/housing_audit.csv")   # read it, name it

audit                                                # print it
```

::: {.small}
What comes back is a **data frame**: a rectangle with one row per observation, here one email, and one column per variable, each column of a single type.

`readr::` names the package that the function comes from. The package must be installed first; that happens once, and the setup page says how.
:::

::: notes
Getting data in. The part before the double colon names the package that the function comes from, here readr, so that you can always see where a function lives; the package has to be installed first, which is a separate step that you do once. Then read underscore csv reads the file and the arrow gives the result a name, so from here on audit is our data. Typing the name on its own prints it. What you get back is a data frame, the central object of R: a rectangle with one row for each email and one column for each variable, every column holding a single type. Nearly every function that you will meet takes a data frame and hands one back, which is why the pipe works so well: the output of one step is the right shape to be the input of the next.
:::

## Inspecting the data {#look-before-you-model .smaller .deepdive run="tools"}

```{.r code-line-numbers="|1|2|3|4"}
datawizard::data_peek(audit)             # every column, its type, the first few values
nrow(audit)                              # 1014
datawizard::data_tabulate(audit$name)    # how many emails went out under each name?
datawizard::data_tabulate(audit$reply)   # 1, 0 – and NA for the emails that bounced
```

::: {.fragment .small}
`NA` is how R marks a missing value. Here it means that an email bounced and never reached anyone, which is a different thing from an email that drew no reply. Most serious errors are visible in the data before they reach a model.
:::

::: notes
With the data loaded, look at them before any model touches them. Data peek shows every column with its type and its first few values. nrow counts the rows, one per email. Data tabulate tells you how many emails went out under each name, which should be roughly equal, because the names were assigned at random. And tabulating the reply column gives you ones, zeros, and a handful of NA. [advance] NA is how R marks a missing value, and in this file it means something specific: the email bounced and never reached an official. That is not the same as an email that drew no reply, and a model that treated the two alike would be measuring a failure of delivery. Every serious error I have made was visible in the data before it reached a model.
:::

## Working with rows and columns {#five-verbs-do-most-of-the-work .smaller .deepdive run="tools"}

```{.r code-line-numbers="|2|3|4|5"}
audit |>
  datawizard::data_filter(reply == 1 & !is.na(named)) |>         # keep the coded replies
  datawizard::data_select(c("name", "group", "named")) |>        # keep three columns
  datawizard::data_modify(hispanic = group == "hispanic") |>     # make a new column
  datawizard::data_arrange("name")                               # sort
```

::: {.fragment .small}
The fifth verb is `data_summary()`, here with `by`: collapse many rows into one per group.

```{.r}
audit |>
  datawizard::data_filter(reply == 1 & !is.na(named)) |>
  datawizard::data_summary(replies = n(), greeted = mean(named), by = "group")
```
:::

::: notes
Four verbs get you a very long way, and they share one pattern: a data frame goes in and a data frame comes out. Data filter keeps rows, here the replies that carry a greeting code. Data select keeps columns. Data modify makes a new column, here a true or false for the Hispanic names. Data arrange sorts. All four come from datawizard, the package of the course for data work. Read it downwards as a sentence: take the emails, then keep the coded replies, then keep three columns, then add a column, then sort by name. [advance] The fifth verb is data summary, which collapses many rows into one per group. These three lines give you, for each group of names, the number of coded replies and the share that greeted the sender by name: the right-hand panel of the figure that you met earlier, as a table.
:::

## Tables and tests {.smaller .deepdive run="tools"}

```{.r code-line-numbers="|1-3|5|6"}
coded_replies <- original |>
  datawizard::data_filter(!is.na(ProperName)) |>
  datawizard::data_modify(hispanic_name = grepl("^Hispanic", TreatmentGroup))

tab_8ptrz <- xtabs(~ hispanic_name + ProperName, data = coded_replies)
chisq.test(tab_8ptrz)
```

::: {.small}
`xtabs()` counts the rows in each combination of two variables, a **cross-tabulation**. `chisq.test()` asks whether the two variables are independent in the table. This is the reproduction of 8PTRZ in Task 3, on the public file of the OAs, whose column names are kept as they were published.
:::

::: notes
Two functions that you will use in Task 3. The first block reads the public file of the original authors, keeps the replies that carry a greeting code, and makes a true or false column for the Hispanic names, using grepl, which asks whether a piece of text matches a pattern; the little hat means "starts with". Then xtabs counts the replies in each combination of two variables, Hispanic name or not and greeted by name or not, which gives a two-by-two table. And chisq dot test asks whether the two variables are independent in that table. That is the whole reproduction of one of the five analysts, 8PTRZ, and the other four put a model or a test of two proportions in place of the table. When you get there, look at the first line of what it prints, because it names something that matters.
:::

## Model formulas {#a-model-is-a-formula-plus-data .smaller .deepdive run="tools"}

```{.r code-line-numbers="|1|3|5"}
named ~ hispanic                                    # "named explained by hispanic"

m <- lm(named ~ hispanic, data = replies)           # a linear model

g <- glm(named ~ hispanic, family = binomial(), data = replies)   # a logit
```

::: {.small}
The tilde `~` reads **outcome on the left, predictors on the right**; add predictors with `+`. Almost every modelling function in R has this shape: `something(formula, data = ...)`.
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
With a 0/1 outcome and a 0/1 predictor, the coefficient of `lm()` **is** the difference between the two shares. Part 3 comes back to both models[, in the reproduction]{.content-visible unless-meta="deck.menu"}.
:::

::: notes
A model in R is a formula plus data, and the tilde is the heart of the formula: outcome on the left, predictors on the right, more predictors added with a plus. Then lm fits a linear model, and glm with the binomial family fits a logistic regression, a logit. Almost every modelling function in R has this same shape, a formula and then data, so once you know it, lm, glm and everything after them become variations on one pattern. [advance] And one fact that makes this case easy to learn on: when the outcome is zero or one and the predictor is zero or one, the coefficient of the linear model is exactly the difference between the two shares. A greeting rate of forty-one per cent against sixty-one gives a coefficient of minus point two. We come back to both models in Part 3[, when you reproduce the analysts]{.content-visible unless-meta="deck.menu"}.
:::

## Plotting with tinyplot {#one-line-of-ggplot .smaller .deepdive run="tools"}

```{.r code-line-numbers="|1-3|4|5"}
greeted <- audit |>
  datawizard::data_filter(reply == 1 & !is.na(named)) |>
  datawizard::data_summary(greeted = mean(named), by = c("name", "group"))
tinyplot::tinyplot(greeted ~ name | group, data = greeted,   # what goes where, coloured by group
                   type = "p", flip = TRUE)                  # draw points, names on the side
```

::: {.small}
Two parts: a **formula**, `y ~ x | group`, with the **data**, which says what goes on which axis and what sets the colour, and a **type** that says what to draw.
:::

::: notes
Plotting, briefly, with tinyplot, the package that draws every figure of your workspace and of the browser lab. First the data: the share of coded replies that greeted the sender by name, for each of the six names, kept in a small table called greeted. Then a tinyplot has two parts. A formula with the data, the same tilde as in a model, which says what goes on which axis, and the vertical bar adds a third variable that sets the colour, here the group that the name was meant to indicate. And a type, which says what to draw: points. Flip turns the chart on its side, so the names can be read. The plot it makes is a rough version of the right-hand panel from earlier.
:::

## Causal graphs in R {#a-causal-graph-is-a-set-of-arrows .smaller .deepdive run="tools"}

```{.r code-line-numbers="|2|3|4-5|6|10|11"}
dag <- make_dag(
  "name -> reply",
  "reply -> greeting",
  "official -> reply", "official -> greeting",
  "community -> reply", "community -> greeting",
  # "name -> greeting",          # the arrow that the claim is about
  exposure = "name", outcome = "greeting", latent = "official"
)

dagitty::adjustmentSets(dag)               # what must be adjusted for?
dagitty::paths(dag, Z = "reply")           # which paths open among the replies?
```

::: {.small}
One arrow per line, written **cause -> effect**, so a `#` takes an arrow out and the code still runs. `make_dag()` is a helper of the workspace, built on **dagitty**.
:::

::: notes
[The last piece of R is the one you use in the next task.]{.content-visible unless-meta="deck.data-tools"}[The last piece of R is one that the other formats of the course use for the causal graph of the experiment, so I take it quickly.]{.content-visible when-meta="deck.data-tools"} A causal graph in the workspace is a list of arrows, one per line, written cause, then an arrow, then effect. The name points at the reply, the reply at the greeting, and the official and the community each point at both. The arrow that the claim is about is commented out with a hash, so that you decide whether to switch it on. You also declare which node is the exposure, which the outcome, and that the official is latent, unobserved. Then two questions for dagitty. adjustmentSets asks what you must adjust for to estimate the effect of the name, and paths, with Z set to the reply, asks which paths between the name and the greeting are open once the comparison is made among the replies.
:::

## Common error messages {#when-it-breaks .smaller .deepdive run="tools"}

::: {.small}
| What you see | What it usually means |
|---|---|
| `could not find function "try_spec"` | The helpers are not loaded – run `source("R/spec_tools.R")` |
| `object 'audit' not found` | You ran this chunk before the one that creates it – go back up and run in order |
| `object 'hispanic_name' not found` | The column does not exist yet – you skipped the `data_modify()` that makes it |
| `+` on the console, nothing happens | An unclosed bracket or quote. Press **Esc** and look for the missing `)` |
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
Read the error. R error messages are terse but almost always literally true, and most of them name the thing that R could not find.
:::

::: notes
These four errors will be most of what you meet in the tasks. "Could not find function" means that the helpers are not loaded or a package is not installed, so source the helper file or install the package. "Object audit not found" means that you ran a chunk before the one that creates the object; go back up and run them in order. "Object hispanic underscore name not found" means that you skipped the data modify line that makes the column. And if the console shows a plus sign and nothing happens, R thinks that you have not finished the command: there is an unclosed bracket or quote somewhere. Press Escape and go looking for it. The general advice is the habit I would most like you to keep: read the error, because it usually names exactly what R could not find.
:::
